newsitem.title: GERMANY: Preussag says 95/96 net down, outlook good.
newsitem.headline: Preussag says 95/96 net down, outlook good.

text.p: German diversified metals and engineering group Preussag AG said on Thursday its net profit fell to 274 million marks ($165.7 million) in the year to September 30 from 349 million marks the year before.
But chairman Michael Frenzel said steel orders and output were rebounding strongly and prices were beginning to follow, and he sees a good outlook for the current year.
"If current trends solidify, Preussag profit will be clearly higher," Frenzel said. The 1995/96 result was better than most analysts' expectations, and better than the first-half trend.

While the upturn in steel prices is still tentative, the company is already benefitting from higher prices for non-ferrous metals, higher oil prices and the stronger dollar, which boosts its mark-denominated revenues from energy products.

"To achieve these positive results, though, we must have a better tendency in steel," said chief financial officer Rainer Feuerhake in an interview with Reuters Television. "We are still not happy with the steel price situation."
Sales in 1995/96 fell slightly to 25.044 billion marks from 26.353 billion marks, while incoming orders dropped to 28.537 billion marks from 30.229 billion marks.

The weak domestic economy, particularly in steel, added to the challenges Preussag faced in building up its international business in 1995/96. The company is counting on cost management to increase profitability, Frenzel said.
Return on capital was 15.2 percent, above the company's target of 15 percent, but Frenzel said he aims to boost that return to 20 percent, without specifying a timeframe.

Frenzel said he was not happy with the company's share price performance, and would continue to boost shareholder value. At midday, Preussag shares were trading five marks up at 393 marks, but down from 419 marks last March.
Orders on hand were a record 13.989 billion marks, up from 13.582 billion marks. The company proposed an unchanged dividend of 12 marks, but profit fell to 17 marks from 28 marks a share.
Acquisitions boosted the workforce to 66,226 from 65,227, but personnel costs declined to 5.441 billion marks from 5.481 billion marks the year before.
In the first quarter of the current business year, Preussag showed a higher profit than in the year-earlier quarter, Frenzel said, without naming a figure.
Sales in the first quarter were 6.3 billion marks, down from 6.8 billion, but Frenzel said sales were higher after correction for an extraordinary item in shipbuilding.
First-quarter incoming orders were 6.1 billion marks, down from 6.3 billion marks, but orders on hand were 13.7 billion marks, up from 13.3 billion marks.

Steel orders were up 20 percent in the quarter ended December, while production rose 35 percent. "Prices followed these trends only hesitantly, but we were able to to raise our prices slightly in the first quarter. Further price rises are planned," Frenzel said.

He said it was too early to give a solid earnings outlook for the steel sector, which contributed only five percent to Preussag's ordinary income in 1995/96 though it employed 21 percent of the workforce. "The crucial factor will be whether we can implement the planned price increases."
Preussag cut 1,100 steel jobs last year, and plans to cut 250 more this year, he said.

In the year ended September 30, crude steel production in Germany shrank 10 percent, while world production fell only one percent. Output in Japan dropped five percent, and in the European Union eight percent, he said.
Preussag said it would focus on logistics, energy and building engineering as growth areas. The three divisions already account for over 50 percent of turnover.
About 50 percent of last year's 1.4 billion marks in investments was earmarked for capacity expansion, primarily in the three key growth areas.
($ = 1.653 German Marks)
